articles.title: Political disconnect
articles.content: THE disconnect between the government and public concerns could not be starker. While people worry about their economic situation the government is focused on altering the country’s provincial structure. According to thelatest Ipsos poll, three in four people believe the country is headed in the wrong direction. The economy and especially inflation are their top concerns. A majority of respondents also said they do not view the economy as strong. It is this low public confidence and pessimism about the future that should concern the government rather than seeking to redraw the provincial map for ill-defined objectives. So far it hasn’t offered any coherent rationale for carving out more provinces. It has also not conducted any study on an issue of such consequence. Although speculation had long been rife about the hybrid government’s intentions it was Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi who made apublic pitch for new provinces in July. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal went further, calling for 15 additional provinces. Each province, he said, should be subdivided into three. As an alternative, he proposed 160 district governments. He argued that establishing more administrative units would deliver effective governance and better social outcomes. The proposal provoked a furious response from the ruling party’s ally, PPP, which opposed any plan to divide Sindh. The party got the Sindh Assembly toadopt a resolutionrejecting the division of the province or creation of new administrative units. The MQM, which has long wanted Karachi as a separate province, boycotted the session. It said its proposals were not incorporated in the resolution, including establishing new administrative units. The resolution declared “Sindh is one and shall remain one” and “unequivocally rejected any proposal, plan, scheme or constitutional arrangement … which sought to divide Sindh … or create any new province out of its territory”. Technical fixes are no panacea that will miraculously solve the country’s problems. The government’s attempt to start a debate seemed to flounder and spin out of control after its key coalition partner came out in strong opposition. A senior PPP leaderquestionedPrime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s silence and asked him to state his position publicly. Another PPP leader accused federal ministers pushing for new provinces of having a “fake mandate”. Meanwhile, PML-N ministers themselves issued contradictory statements. Rather than clarifying matters, this compounded the confusion and exposed divisions within the party. Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz is also said to be opposed to any division of her province. The joint parliamentary opposition comprising PTI, JUI-F and other smaller partiesrejectedany plan to divide provinces at its inaugural meeting in late August. Earlier, JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman argued this was not the time to divide provinces given the country’s troubled economic and security situation. PTI is now planning a multiparty conference of the opposition on the issue. The party itself has yet to enunciate a clear public position. In the past, it advocated creating a new province in south Punjab. Some PTI leaders say the party opposes changes under “an illegitimate and fraudulent set-up”. The party chairman, however, has urged consultations and said any hasty decision would “harm the federation”. Meanwhile, the leader of the National Party in Balochistan has said creating new provinces would only exacerbate present tensions. None of this has deterred federal ministers from continuing to insist on administrative restructuring. Mohsin Naqvideclaredthis was essential and no one can stop it. But he added it will only happen with the “will of the people”. He wasn’t walking back from his proposal. His statement implied a referendum might be held to ascertain the ‘will of the people’. Such a move would be deeply controversial and divisive. It would also lack credibility given the history of dubious referendums conducted by past military governments. Questions have also been raised about whether a referendum can constitutionally be used to create new provinces. Proponents of ‘reform’ in the hybrid government ignore the fact that their proposal has already divided the country. It is clear that there is no political consensus on the issue. Consensus cannot be manufactured or coerced. While the government has rammed controversial constitutional amendments and other laws through parliament, using the same method to reorder the provincial structure carries much greater risks. Given the far-reaching consequences of the change and the opposition it faces across the country, the implications would be serious. If pursued, it would further undermine national cohesion and deepen polarisation. There is a clear constitutional procedure to change provincial boundaries. A referendum cannot override that. Any change requires two steps. First a resolution passed by a two-thirds majority in the relevant provincial assembly. Second a constitutional amendment adopted by a two-thirds majority in both the National Assembly and Senate. This effectively gives affected provinces a veto over any change. This requirement cannot be bypassed. Any political manoeuvre to circumvent this will be a disaster. There is no doubt that the governance system needs to be improved. Government should be brought closer to the people to ensure their voices are heard and for better service delivery. But this goal can be realised by empowering local government. It is the third tier of government that needs to be strengthened through functional local bodies as mandated by the Constitution. Improving governance requires more than a technical fix. Above all, it demands an environment grounded in the rule of law. It needs accountability of both leaders and institutions. Administrative changes cannot substitute for competent leadership — with a clear vision and sense of purpose — who are legitimately elected. Good governance also requires prudent policies and much-needed economic reforms shaped and overseen by capable professionals. This is not an argument against administrative change. It is an effort to emphasise three points. First, drawing new provincial lines is not a panacea that will miraculously solve the country’s problems. As noted above, other aspects of governance matter far more. Map-drawing and not fixing fundamentals is meaningless. Second, such changes do not figure among the public’s governance concerns, which are very different. Ignoring those priorities and focusing just on technical fixes will only show how out of touch the government is with people. Third, without broad national consensus, imposing administrative changes will make a mockery of democracy and serve to divide the country. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: Extraction and delivery
articles.content: AS the debate on changing provincial boundaries and decentralisation rages on, it is worth taking a step back to see what is at stake here. What are the main problems that require attention and which have made several people, including entrenched insiders,declare that the current system is ‘broken’? The biggest issue being sidestepped by everyone involved (except opposition parties) remains constitutional rule and legitimacy of the state. The current discourse chooses to ignore this, considering it either taboo or a foregone conclusion. Bringing it up seems particularly futile in this discussion given how little it bears on those making decisions and increasingly with those tasked with interrogating these decisions. The second issue is macroeconomic growth, or the absence thereof. What changes are needed to the form of the state that can help kickstart broad-based and sustained capital accumulation? What needs to be done to make the state fiscally more viable? The third issue is social development, and the slowdown in improvement of basic education, health, and other human capability-related indicators. What strategy or approach will help break through the current plateau, marked by a slowdown in literacy rate improvement, a persistently large number of out-of-school children, poor learning outcomes, and no considerable progress on health indicators? When the interior minister talks about a system collapse, the primary subject of this collapse is the state. The Pakistani state, like every other modern state, is engaged in a variety of tasks, none of which it seems to be doing too well. Broadly these tasks can be clubbed under two domains — extraction (getting something from its population) and delivery (doing something for or to the population). There is a third domain — regulation (setting boundaries or implementing rules for various things that private actors may be doing) — as well but we’ll keep that to one side for now. There is no one-size-fits-all approach for the many developmental challenges confronting Pakistan today. The historical record on extraction and delivery is generally poor. Extracting taxes from anyone other than a captive population has proven to be a challenge. Regulating private behaviour, from polluting emissions to urban sprawl to inter-gender interactions, has been difficult as well. And delivering basic services — law and order, education, health — remains highly uneven across rural-urban and provincial lines. If one thinks about the state as the core of a governing system, the track record so far provides ample grounds for a complete overhaul. But a key question to ask is: do all of these functions require an overhaul of the same type? It is possible to look at the exceedingly few examples of success on part of the state in each domain as a blueprint of sorts for what works, especially when thinking about administrative changes. What type of extraction has the state done well and where has it failed? In recent years, the state has done a ‘good’ job of getting people to pay for expensive electricity at cost, rather than delay tariff revisions or provide blanket subsidies. This is an example of a reform that is not really productivity enhancing, but it is certainly something that the state was not doing a decade and a half ago. Similarly, the state has been successful at extracting more taxes from the formal sector and the salaried segment of the population in recent years. This is both by raising the tax rate and by making it ever difficult for the formal sector to avoid its share through an entrenched withholding tax regime. This has happened even while the state has failed to bring many sections of the population into the tax net. When we review the evidence on what enables some types of extraction over others, the absence of discretion and fragmentation of functions comes out as a possible factor. In the case of electricity bills and withholding taxes, the state has centralised collection and removed discretion from its own functions. Local state functionaries have some leeway, sure, but by and large people have no option but to comply and pay directly to the state. In contrast, where economic activity has to be documented by state functionaries themselves (ie, a situation of increased discretion) local politics and influence come into play. On the other hand, the evidence on delivery points in the opposite direction. The biggest gains in social development took place during times of greater decentralisation. When schools were being managed at the school council/local level, improvements in literacy rates and enrolment happened at a faster rate. Similarly, greater autonomy for basic health units and hospitals (with requisite oversight) allowed them to respond to actual patient-level challenges more effectively. Even in delivering basic municipal infrastructure — sanitation and sewage, roadworks — decentralised decision-making and expenditure (between 2002-2008) proved to be more effective. Since province-level centralisation took hold in 2011, gains in key delivery areas of health and education have slowed down. In some parts of the country, outcomes have stagnated altogether. The challenge of delivering to hard-to-access populations has become far more acute. Given this admittedly speculative review of patterns in both extraction and delivery, it is clear there is no one-size-fits-all approach for the many developmental challenges confronting Pakistan today. In domains of extraction, there is an urgent need to reduce discretion and fragmentation of state authority, perhaps even with the use of automated structures in whatever form. In delivery related domains, we likely need even more discretion and fragmentation of the state, via substantive decentralisation that devolves decision-making and accountability down to the level where delivery is supposed to take place. The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums.
articles.author: Umair Javed

articles.title: Road to dignity
articles.content: IN Pakistan’s recent history, billionaire bankers and former staff of multilateral institutions, among others, have led national development. After assuming office as finance minister, one was alleged to have declared that he empathised with ordinary people and then promptly imposed a tax on baby food in a country where, due to malnutrition, 40 per cent of children are stunted. The results are hardly what we had hoped for. How, then, should national development policy be made? Let us take a hypothetical case of a recently formed country, its borders determined by departing colonialists. It is not a ‘civilisational state’ with thousands of years of shared history, so the allegiance and love of its people should now be earned. There must be a clear rationale for forming the new country. A civilised society might agree that its rationale is the welfare of its citizens: people come together to improve their standard of living, to have equal opportunity to reach their full potential, and to live by their values. The citizens are to pay a share of their income to a common fund, from which the state would administer services to all, such as education, healthcare, support for economic endeavour and security. The country must be sovereign and independent. If the former colonialists offered to guide and direct the new country’s development, surely they would be spurned: after 200 years of ruthless exploitation, they could hardly be trusted. While the people’s priorities are likely to be efficient agriculture and affordable food, quality education and skills training, healthcare and economic development, outsiders might want to prioritise gender issues and preparedness for future disasters. Policy must be made by those who represent the people. Conventionally, to pay for imports such as oil, gas and advanced machinery, a country has to earn international currency through exports. If imports were double the exports, that would be untenable. The country would then have to take loans from foreign sources on conditions that absolutely compromise its sovereignty. Even multilateral institutions have voting systems firmly controlled by the West. At the IMF, for instance, Pakistan has 0.43pc of the vote, Russia 2.59pc, China 6.08pc, and the US 16.5pc, besides the votes of all its ‘loyal allies’. To be sovereign, the country would focus its exports on markets where its products — including new ones beyond traditional leather goods, towels and the like — were more likely to find acceptance. A developing country’s products are more likely to be accepted in the Global South, among other developing countries that are more price-sensitive and less demanding about quality. It should try to exchange goods in national currencies or through a swap arrangement. The country would not implore its former colonial masters to grant it limited market access — as a great favour — that could be rescinded over any supposed breach, with sanctions imposed. The country would encourage innovative, efficient and cost-effective production. Open and fair competition would bring forward businesspeople capable of competing internationally. Surely, ‘crony’ business groups with no merit beyond maintaining relationships with decision-makers would not be tolerated. Nor would rules be made or changed to benefit particular businesspeople, or unjustified subsidies and concessions be granted to them. Where a subsidy was justified, proportionate shares and profits would go to the state. Taking full advantage of its border with a great power — the world’s manufacturing centre — the developing country would offer every facility to serve as a goods-processing hub, especially in its coastal regions. The key lessons are clear: policy ought to be made by people who understand and represent the people, not by narrowly focused technical specialists. A country’s national development policy must be predicated on an agreed direction — its rationale, and the people’s priorities, needs and values. Not foreign donor agendas. The country’s economic transformation requires open and fair business competition. ‘Cronyism’ sabotages it. Focus exports on the Global South and make every effort to exchange goods in national currencies or through similar arrangements. Especially in the coastal zones, offer every facility for goods processing from the bordering great power. Incentivise officials by aligning promotions with the performance of the areas they serve. This is a time of great opportunity for the Global South. The global power balance and systems are changing — a change so fundamental that nothing comparable has happened in hundreds of years. Pakistan must tailor its public policy to the changing environment to achieve its national development goals and pursue national sovereignty and dignity. The writer is the author of Pakistan: Principles of Public Policy Redefined.
articles.author: Zafar U. Ahmed

articles.title: Showing empathy
articles.content: ON the 100-day anniversary of the Oct 7, 2023, attack by Hamas against Israel, and after 25,000 Palestinians had been killed by Israel’s retaliatory strikes, then US president Joe Biden made a shocking statement: “I will never forget the grief and the suffering I have heard in my meetings with the families of the American hostages. No one should have to endure even one day of what they have gone through, much less 100.” His statement did not reference the thousands of slaughtered Palestinians, including women and children, or the intentional targeting of hospitals and journalists. Nor did it acknowledge the International Court of Justice hearings that had begun days prior to investigate allegations of Israeli war crimes. The statement was derided as “shameful” by Barnett Rubin, a US foreign policy expert who knew Biden from their time in the Obama administration. Biden’s one-sided statement is flagged in a new book, Crossing the Red Line, by award-winning Pakistani journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed, which documents how the Biden administration enabled Israeli atrocities in Gaza, and set the stage for the widening of the Middle East conflict during the current Trump administration. In a book filled with examples of US negligence and complicity in breaches of international law in Gaza, this example resonates. Speaking last week at a book launch event, Ahmed used the example to illustrate Biden’s tunnel vision when it came to the Israel-Palestine conflict, specifically his inability to acknowledge the plight of Palestinians. In Biden’s and his administration’s perspective, all Palestinian children killed were the children of Hamas fighters; reports of famine in Gaza were exaggerated; schools and hospitals were Hamas hideouts; and intelligence or humanitarian reports suggesting otherwise were forced to caveat findings or report selectively. The need for engagement is too often simplified. The president’s inability to humanise Palestinians or empathise with their predicament was, Ahmed argued, a determinant of the US’s Israel policy and its failure to curtail Israeli transgressions. He highlighted a key reason for this lack of empathy: the US administration barely had any interaction with Palestinians. Although there was robust engagement with Israelis, Ahmed reports there were only five State Department officials in direct contact with Palestinians. Of all the avoidable tragedies Ahmed’s work highlights, the fact that you need to talk to people on the other side of a conflict to remember that they are human, truly resonates. That recognition of humanity is then enshrined in policy and decision-making. This need for engagement is too often simplified and understood as the need for backchannels during a crisis. No doubt, informal, person-to-person contact is invaluable when de-escalation is required. Recall the secret meetings that avoided nuclear war during the Cuban Missile Crisis or — closer to home — the DGMO hotline that prevented the May 2025 Pakistan-India conflict from escalating further. But backchannels cannot substitute for broader diplomatic and societal engagement, the type that goes past mere coordination to empathic connection; the type the Americans have in place with Israel, but did not bother to develop with Palestine, even at the height of humanitarian crisis during the darkest days of the Gaza war. It is a point that should be emphasised in the context of mainstream diplomacy at a time when most Western governments are reducing global diplomatic staff and closing embassies, usually as a cost-cutting measure, leaving them with few personal touch points in regions in perma-crisis. But these lessons also apply domestically. The political polarisation of Western countries is increasingly attributed to a breakdown of engagement between urban and rural residents, the rich and the poor, and between different racial and ethnic communities. This, in turn, is blamed on everything from the isolation wrought by social media to the claw-back of government funding for community spaces. We are not absolved from complicity closer to home. It is difficult to imagine Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz making the divisive comments she did about threats to Punjab primarily emanating from regional provinces without years of political suppression and polarised rhetoric between provinces, particularly with Balochistan and KP. Without more access and engagement, compatriots cannot empathise with each other’s challenges. That engagement should be encouraged across all levels of provincial governments, but equally across society, whether in the form of more scholarships, economic ties, tourism, arts engagement or the lifting of media censorship. Without engaging, we’re in danger of forgetting each other’s humanity, and so exacerbating rather than allaying tensions. The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.
articles.author: Huma Yusuf

articles.title: Inflation, again
articles.content: WITH petrol and diesel pricesrising at a steady clip, households are bracing for another round of caustic price increases that burn into monthly budgets and force further belt-tightening. TheSensitive Price Indicator, the weekly inflation gauge published by the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics, was up 8.62pc for the week ended Sept 10 compared to a year ago. Onions, a staple in the local cuisine, had more than doubled in price. Fuel was sharply up: LPG 55pc dearer, and diesel and petrol costing 45pc and 39pc more, respectively, than a year ago. Wheat, another staple, was up 30pc from last year; electricity bills were higher by 25pc. Beef, mutton and chillies were also up by double digits. It bears putting these numbers into perspective: the SPI is deliberately weighted towards tracking daily-use essentials that matter most to lower- and lower-middle-income households. In other words, these numbers represent the cost-of-living squeeze on ordinary Pakistanis. Wages for the vast majority do not keep pace with inflation, which means ordinary people must adjust the only way they can: by reducing usage and consumption. As it is, the inflationary storm unleashed on Pakistan from 2022 onwards has set the vast majority years back in terms of quality of life. Recent statistics show that people are eating less than they did to make ends meet, which is in itself a startling indication of how badly the last bout of prolonged inflation affected households across the country. There has been demand destruction at immense scale, and the local economy may struggle for years to escape this trap. The recent price pressures appear to be driven by theunending war in the Persian Gulf, which has roiled global markets for months now and affected Pakistan particularly intensely due to the country’s dependency on Gulf markets for its energy needs. And there is no indication it will end soon. It is unfortunate that the government has yet to confront the challenge publicly, or show more than a cursory concern for the hardships of ordinary citizens. Granted global oil prices are not in its control, but there are other things it can do. Though the topic now seems taboo, it can still cut the petroleum levy to give relief; all it needs to do is fund the revenue shortfall from another means. It can squeeze undertaxed sectors that have traditionally enjoyed broad exemptions due to political reasons. Authorities must also monitor the produce markets closely and step in to prevent hoarding and profiteering when needed. Inflation has a steep political cost, and lack of visible action will hurt the government in more ways than one. Silence cannot be a policy: at the very least, the citizenry needs an acknowledgment of the challenges they face and a plan to mitigate them.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: What may be said
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S press freedom crisis is no longer something that can be dismissed as routine criticism. When nine rights and media organisations — including the Committee to Protect Journalists, Reporters Without Borders, the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan and the International Federation for Human Rights — warn Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of a “rapidly deteriorating” environment, the alarm deserves a substantive response. Their concerns are specific: journalists have disappeared, faced detention and criminal investigations, been obstructed from reporting in parts of the country, and, allegedly under official pressure, lost jobs or been removed from air. The growing use of Peca and investigations by the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency have reinforced fears that laws framed to counter cybercrime and false information are being used to police journalism. Restrictions in AJK, internet and telecommunications blackouts, curbs on foreign correspondents, action against broadcasters, the blocking of Al Jazeera’s website, and allegations of pressure surrounding the removal of journalists from television all point to shrinking space for independent reporting. The government must recognise that invoking national security, public order or misinformation cannot provide open-ended justification for curbing legitimate public-interest journalism. What is required now is action. The government should ensure the safe return of journalists Razi Tahir and Muhammad Saif, order transparent investigations into attacks such as that on reporter Mian Zahid Owaisi, and make the findings public. Allegations that state agencies or officials have pressured media organisations should be independently examined, while regulatory action against broadcasters must follow transparent legal processes. Curbs on foreign media and access to information should be reviewed and withdrawn where they cannot be justified. Most importantly, the government must revisit provisions of Peca that can be deployed against legitimate journalism and create safeguards against their misuse. The PM should convene media bodies, rights groups and legal experts to develop such protections and require accountability from agencies accused of intimidation. Press freedom is not a favour extended by the state. It is a constitutional safeguard and a prerequisite for democratic accountability. Pakistan’s journalists need due process, access to information, protection from coercion and an unequivocal commitment that critical reporting will not be treated as a crime.
articles.author: Editorial
